title: The Tribes Restored and the City Named The LORD Is There
summary: The land is divided into twelve equal strips running east to west, seven tribes to the north and five to the south of a central holy portion. That portion holds the sanctuary with the priests' land, the Levites' land, and the city with its farmland, flanked by the prince's estate. The city has twelve gates named for the tribes of Israel, and from that day its name will be The LORD Is There.
story: This is the last chapter of Ezekiel and the end of its great temple vision (chapters 40 to 48). The book began with the prophet among the exiles by the Kebar canal, seeing the glory of God far from Jerusalem, and it traced that glory's departure from the defiled temple and city (chapters 10 and 11). It ends with the whole people restored to the land, arranged around God's dwelling, and a city whose very name declares that God has come home. The tribal list recalls the division of the land under Joshua, but everything is redrawn around the sanctuary. The story of Ezekiel, which moved from judgment to hope, closes on a single word of promise: there. God will be there, with his people, for good.
historical:
The tribal allotments are unlike any historical map of Israel. Under Joshua the tribes received territories of different sizes and shapes, some east of the Jordan. Ezekiel gives each tribe an equal strip stretching from the western sea to the eastern border (47:14), all west of the Jordan. The order is also new. The tribes descended from Jacob's sons by the servant women Bilhah and Zilpah (Dan, Naphtali, Asher, and Gad) are placed at the far north and far south, while Judah and Benjamin, the tribes that had remained loyal to the temple in Jerusalem, sit nearest the holy portion. Reuben, Jacob's firstborn who lost his birthright (Genesis 49:3-4), is restored to a place next to Judah. The holy portion lies roughly where Jerusalem had been, but it stands between tribes rather than within one.

When Ezekiel received this vision, about 573 BC, the ten northern tribes had been scattered for about 150 years, and Judah was in exile. The vision imagines all twelve reunited, as chapter 37 had promised with the sign of two sticks joined into one. When exiles later returned under Persian rule, they rebuilt a temple in Jerusalem (completed about 516 BC), but neither that temple nor Herod's later expansion followed Ezekiel's plan, and the land was never divided in this way.
cultural:
Land in Israel was not simply property. Each family's inheritance was held from God, who said that "The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine" (Leviticus 25:23). Equal portions for the tribes express the equality of God's people under him, and the holy land of the Levites cannot be sold or exchanged (verse 14), because it belongs to the LORD. The city is set in the common portion rather than the holy one, and it is worked by people from all the tribes (verse 19). It is a shared city, not the possession of one tribe or one dynasty, which is a pointed contrast with Jerusalem as the city of David.

City gates in the ancient world were the place of public life, where elders sat, courts met, and trade happened. Naming twelve gates after the twelve tribes means every tribe has its own entrance and its own place in the city's life. Levi, which has no tribal land, receives a gate, and Ephraim and Manasseh share one under the name of their father Joseph, which keeps the number at twelve. The city measures 4,500 cubits on each side, about one and a half miles (2.3 kilometers) using the long cubit, with a perimeter of about six miles.
literary: The chapter is a list, and its form carries meaning. The tribal allotments are recorded in a repetitive formula, one portion from the east side to the west side, that stresses equality and order. The list runs from the northern border down to the holy portion (verses 1 to 7), describes the central portion in detail (verses 8 to 22), and continues from the holy portion to the southern border (verses 23 to 29), placing the sanctuary at the literal center of the text as well as of the land. The final section describes the city's gates in a symmetrical pattern of three on each side (verses 30 to 34). Then the book's last sentence gives the city its name. Ezekiel, which opened with the heavens opening by the Kebar canal, ends with a name for a city in which God dwells.

outline.t: The holy portion for the sanctuary, the priests, and the Levites
The city and its common land
The twelve gates and the city's name

doctrines.note: The book ends with God's presence as its final word: The LORD Is There. The goal of Ezekiel's whole message of judgment and restoration is not a building or a territory but God dwelling with his people.

The land is divided among all twelve tribes, fulfilling the promises to the patriarchs (47:14) and the hope of a reunited people (37:15-28). God keeps faith with the whole of Israel, including the tribes long scattered.
The vision is written to exiles with no temple, no land, and no king. It gives them a future in concrete detail, so that hope has a shape and not only a feeling.

words.note: Sham, there, which becomes part of the city's name in verse 35: YHWH Shammah, The LORD Is There. The simple adverb carries the whole book's hope. The glory that left the city (11:23) is now permanently there.

Cheleq, portion or share. Each tribe receives one portion of equal size. The word is used elsewhere of God himself as the portion of the faithful (Psalm 16:5), a reminder that the land was always a gift that pointed beyond itself.

Chol, common, used in verse 15 for the city's land, which is for common use rather than holy. Common does not mean sinful but ordinary. The vision orders the land so that holy and common each have their place, and ordinary life is lived near God's presence.

Sha'ar, gate. The city has twelve gates named for the tribes (verses 31 to 34), so every tribe has its own way in. Revelation 21:12 describes the new Jerusalem with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes.

christ: The New Testament announces that the presence Ezekiel longed for has come in Jesus: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14), and his name is Immanuel, "God with us" (Matthew 1:23). Through the Spirit, the church is being built into "a dwelling place for God" (Ephesians 2:22). Revelation's closing vision draws heavily on Ezekiel 40 to 48: a city that lies foursquare, with twelve gates named for the tribes of Israel, a river of life, and the voice declaring that "the dwelling place of God is with man" (Revelation 21:3). But John adds a startling detail: "I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple" (Revelation 21:22). The whole city has become what Ezekiel's sanctuary was. Christians read the name The LORD Is There as fulfilled in Christ now and completely in the new creation.

hard.q: Will Ezekiel's temple actually be built?
hard.a: Faithful readers answer differently. Many dispensational premillennialists expect a literal temple to be built in a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth, with the land divided as described; they point to the vision's detailed measurements and to promises made to Israel as a nation, and many of them see any sacrifices there as memorials rather than atonements. Some scholars read chapters 40 to 48 as a program for the restoration after the exile, an ideal that the returning community did not carry out. Many Christian interpreters, in the Reformed and other traditions, read the vision as symbolic or typological: a picture of God dwelling with a purified people, fulfilled in Christ, in the church as God's temple, and finally in the new creation, which Revelation 21 and 22 describe in Ezekiel's own imagery. Some combine these views. The question involves broader convictions about the millennium and about Israel and the church, which are second-order matters on which Christians disagree. All agree on the vision's center: God will dwell with his people.

questions: Each tribe received an equal portion and its own gate, including tribes that had been marginal or scattered. What does that suggest about the place of the overlooked in God's people?
The city is not named for a king or a founder but for God's presence. What would it mean for your home, church, or community to be known above all by that name?
Ezekiel's book moves from God's glory leaving to God's glory dwelling. Where have you experienced the absence of God, and what hope does this ending offer?
